{"title":"A Workflow for Identifying Viable Crystal Structures with Partially Occupied Sites Applied to Solid Electrolyte: Cubic Li 7 La 3 Zr 2 O 12","authors":"Julian Holland; Tom Demeyere; Arihant Bhandari; Felix Hanke; Victor Milman; Chris-Kriton Skylaris","field_subfield":"Materials Science / Computational Chemistry (Solid-State Ionics)","type_of_paper":"Methodology + Case Study (preprint)","executive_summary":"Solid electrolytes are central to next-generation Li-ion batteries, and cubic Li 7 La 3 Zr 2 O 12 (c-LLZO) is regarded as the most interfacially stable fast-ion conductor against metallic Li. However, c-LLZO is not stable at room temperature and is stabilised via substitutional dopants, and there is no consensus on the Li occupancy of its 24d and 96h crystallographic sites. Prior computational studies typically start from one experimental occupancy value to build an idealised unit cell, but the wide range of reported structures indicates disagreement about the ground state, and properties derived from such structures may be poorly described if they are not near the ground state. The authors present a workflow to identify energetically favourable configurations of c-LLZO for a crystallographically predicted structure. They begin by eliminating structures involving overlapping Li atoms based on nearest-neighbour counts, using a minimal Li–Li distance of 1.7 Å (below twice the ionic radius of Li and below the minimum t-LLZO distance of 2.56 Å). They then reduce the configuration space by eliminating symmetry images from all remaining structures using local sensitive hashing (LSH), which scales the pairwise comparison from O(N 2 ) to O(N ) and enables symmetry checks on over 100 million structures. This reduces the space to approximately 2 × 10 6 symmetry-unique structures. They then perform 1235 single-point DFT calculations with the ONETEP code (PBE functional, 830 eV kinetic energy cutoff) on two subsets: the 200 lowest-energy structures according to the COMPASSIII forcefield and a random selection of ~1000 structures. The DFT energies are paired with a numerical representation of the structure (a frequency occurrence list of all possible Li–Li interactions) and fit using a multiple linear regression (MLR) model, with data split into test and training sets at a 1:3 ratio. The model achieves a correlation of 0.9996 on the test set. All structures occur within a range of 5.8 eV of the lowest-energy structure. Nineteen of the 20 lowest-energy structures have a ratio of 8:48, with the 19th lowest being 9:47. The average energy for all structures is 1.47 eV higher than the ground state, and the average energy for each ratio increases with increasing 24d occupancy, indicating an energetic preference to avoid 24d occupation. Four structures, all 8:48, lie within 0.026 eV (1 kT at 298 K) of the lowest-energy structure, and geometry optimisation narrows the energy gap further. The authors note that their energetic ordering procedure does not include entropic contributions and assumes reasonable retention of ordering upon geometry relaxation. They conclude that a large proportion of experimental and theoretical literature may be predicting or working with structures that are not reflective of a real system, and they provide all generated structures in a freely accessible database to improve accuracy and reproducibility. summary.title: A Workflow for Identifying Viable Crystal Structures with Partially Occupied Sites Applied to Solid Electrolyte: Cubic Li 7 La 3 Zr 2 O 12
summary.authors: Julian Holland; Tom Demeyere; Arihant Bhandari; Felix Hanke; Victor Milman; Chris-Kriton Skylaris
summary.executive_summary: Solid electrolytes are central to next-generation Li-ion batteries, and cubic Li 7 La 3 Zr 2 O 12 (c-LLZO) is regarded as the most interfacially stable fast-ion conductor against metallic Li. However, c-LLZO is not stable at room temperature and is stabilised via substitutional dopants, and there is no consensus on the Li occupancy of its 24d and 96h crystallographic sites. Prior computational studies typically start from one experimental occupancy value to build an idealised unit cell, but the wide range of reported structures indicates disagreement about the ground state, and properties derived from such structures may be poorly described if they are not near the ground state. The authors present a workflow to identify energetically favourable configurations of c-LLZO for a crystallographically predicted structure. They begin by eliminating structures involving overlapping Li atoms based on nearest-neighbour counts, using a minimal Li–Li distance of 1.7 Å (below twice the ionic radius of Li and below the minimum t-LLZO distance of 2.56 Å). They then reduce the configuration space by eliminating symmetry images from all remaining structures using local sensitive hashing (LSH), which scales the pairwise comparison from O(N 2 ) to O(N ) and enables symmetry checks on over 100 million structures. This reduces the space to approximately 2 × 10 6 symmetry-unique structures. They then perform 1235 single-point DFT calculations with the ONETEP code (PBE functional, 830 eV kinetic energy cutoff) on two subsets: the 200 lowest-energy structures according to the COMPASSIII forcefield and a random selection of ~1000 structures. The DFT energies are paired with a numerical representation of the structure (a frequency occurrence list of all possible Li–Li interactions) and fit using a multiple linear regression (MLR) model, with data split into test and training sets at a 1:3 ratio. The model achieves a correlation of 0.9996 on the test set. All structures occur within a range of 5.8 eV of the lowest-energy structure. Nineteen of the 20 lowest-energy structures have a ratio of 8:48, with the 19th lowest being 9:47. The average energy for all structures is 1.47 eV higher than the ground state, and the average energy for each ratio increases with increasing 24d occupancy, indicating an energetic preference to avoid 24d occupation. Four structures, all 8:48, lie within 0.026 eV (1 kT at 298 K) of the lowest-energy structure, and geometry optimisation narrows the energy gap further. The authors note that their energetic ordering procedure does not include entropic contributions and assumes reasonable retention of ordering upon geometry relaxation. They conclude that a large proportion of experimental and theoretical literature may be predicting or working with structures that are not reflective of a real system, and they provide all generated structures in a freely accessible database to improve accuracy and reproducibility. The method could be extended to other ion conductors and partially occupied crystals.

claims.description: A workflow can identify energetically favourable configurations of c-LLZO, enabling the isolation of low-energy structures for a crystallographically predicted structure.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
Solid electrolytes are central to next-generation Li-ion batteries, and cubic Li 7 La 3 Zr 2 O 12 (c-LLZO) is regarded as the most interfacially stable fast-ion conductor against metallic Li. However, c-LLZO is not stable at room temperature and is stabilised via substitutional dopants, and there is no consensus on the Li occupancy of its 24d and 96h crystallographic sites. Prior computational studies typically start from one experimental occupancy value to build an idealised unit cell, but the wide range of reported structures indicates disagreement about the ground state, and properties derived from such structures may be poorly described if they are not near the ground state. The authors present a workflow to identify energetically favourable configurations of c-LLZO for a crystallographically predicted structure. They begin by eliminating structures involving overlapping Li atoms based on nearest-neighbour counts, using a minimal Li–Li distance of 1.7 Å (below twice the ionic radius of Li and below the minimum t-LLZO distance of 2.56 Å). They then reduce the configuration space by eliminating symmetry images from all remaining structures using local sensitive hashing (LSH), which scales the pairwise comparison from O(N 2 ) to O(N ) and enables symmetry checks on over 100 million structures. This reduces the space to approximately 2 × 10 6 symmetry-unique structures. They then perform 1235 single-point DFT calculations with the ONETEP code (PBE functional, 830 eV kinetic energy cutoff) on two subsets: the 200 lowest-energy structures according to the COMPASSIII forcefield and a random selection of ~1000 structures. The DFT energies are paired with a numerical representation of the structure (a frequency occurrence list of all possible Li–Li interactions) and fit using a multiple linear regression (MLR) model, with data split into test and training sets at a 1:3 ratio. The model achieves a correlation of 0.9996 on the test set. All structures occur within a range of 5.8 eV of the lowest-energy structure. Nineteen of the 20 lowest-energy structures have a ratio of 8:48, with the 19th lowest being 9:47. The average energy for all structures is 1.47 eV higher than the ground state, and the average energy for each ratio increases with increasing 24d occupancy, indicating an energetic preference to avoid 24d occupation. Four structures, all 8:48, lie within 0.026 eV (1 kT at 298 K) of the lowest-energy structure, and geometry optimisation narrows the energy gap further. The authors note that their energetic ordering procedure does not include entropic contributions and assumes reasonable retention of ordering upon geometry relaxation. They conclude that a large proportion of experimental and theoretical literature may be predicting or working with structures that are not reflective of a real system, and they provide all generated structures in a freely accessible database to improve accuracy and reproducibility. The method could be extended to other ion conductors and partially occupied crystals.

Research Context
The motivation is that solid electrolytes promise higher energy density, improved safety, longer lifetimes, and reduced production costs compared to liquid electrolytes. Electrochemical and chemomechanical stability remain significant issues, with dendrite formation causing short-circuits even for the most stable solid electrolytes. c-LLZO has the best interfacial stability of all popular fast ion conducting solid electrolytes against metallic Li, making it a prominent candidate. c-LLZO is not stable at room temperature but has been stabilised with a number of substitutional dopants on 24d sites. There is no consensus on c-LLZO's Li occupancy, as indicated by the disagreement across reported structures. Prior computational studies often use one experimental occupancy value as a starting point to obtain an idealised unit cell. Without knowing if structures are close to the ground state, more complicated thermodynamic and observable properties may not be well described. The wide range of predicted structures in the literature indicates disagreement about the ground state. The number of ways to populate 120 sites with 56 Li is approximately 7.4 × 10 34, rendering brute-force combinatorial methods unviable. The method could be extended to other ion conductors and partially occupied crystals.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is how to identify and rank all possible Li site occupancies of c-LLZO to find the ground state configuration. The authors intend to produce all possible structures of a c-LLZO unit cell and order them energetically to ascertain a significant energy difference in choice of structure. The authors hope to determine whether structural properties, such as the 24d :96h ratio, are indicative of a structure's energy. The authors neglect to include the 48g site because it is not reported in most refinements. The hypothesis is that imposing a minimal Li–Li distance limits the physically possible 24d :96h ratios. A maximum of 48 out of 96h sites can be occupied at any one time, since each 96h site exists as a pair within 0.68 Å of each other. Each 24d occupation eliminates 4 out of 96h sites as they are within 1.67 Å of this site. The hypothesis is that the majority of energetic changes are due to Li placement, so an expression of all types of Li interactions would be a sufficient descriptor. The hypothesis is that a multiple linear regression model fit to DFT energies can energetically order structures with high accuracy. The hypothesis is that a large proportion of experimental and theoretical literature predicts or works with structures not reflective of a real system. The authors tested whether including the symmetry of the structure in the MLR model made a difference, hypothesising it would be negligible. The authors hypothesised that coulombic forces alone are not sufficient to energetically order c-LLZO structures.

Methodological Details
The study focuses on cubic Li 7 La 3 Zr 2 O 12 (c-LLZO), which has a Hermann-Maguin space group of Ia 3d with Li atoms partially occupying the 24d and 96h sites. The 24d site is tetrahedral and the 96h site occurs at a tetrahedral/octahedral interface. The authors use the crystal structure sites reported by Buschmann et al. as their framework to perform generation. The authors use a minimal Li–Li distance of 1.7 Å, which is less than 2 times the ionic radius of a Li atom and smaller than the minimum distance in t-LLZO (2.56 Å). Any minimal distance between 1.67 Å and 2.3 Å would be suitable for a numerical implementation. The authors generate all possible 24d permutations for a given 24d occupancy, eliminating directly neighbouring 96h sites from consideration. The authors populate the remaining 96h sites such that no two nearest neighbours are occupied simultaneously. The number of structures for each 24d :96h ratio, for one unit cell, are given in Table 1. The authors construct the upper triangular connectivity matrix of the Li sub-lattice for each structure to reduce the data set to unique conformations. The connectivity matrix is defined as the distances between each Li atom to every other Li atom, then flattened and sorted to ensure uniformity. The authors use local sensitive hashing (LSH) to perform fast approximate similarity searches with lower memory requirements than unhashed data. The use of LSH optimises the pairwise comparison from scaling at O(N 2 ) to O(N ), where N is the number of structures.

Procedures And Architectures
The authors initially generate all possible 24d permutations for a given 24d occupancy, eliminating directly neighbouring 96h sites from consideration. The authors populate the remaining 96h sites such that no two nearest neighbours are occupied simultaneously. The method generates all possible structures, approximately 2.3 × 10 8, including symmetry-equivalent duplicates. The authors use LSH to perform symmetry checks on over 100 million structures in a reasonable time frame and attainable memory requirements. Only approximately 1% of structures are symmetrically unique, allowing a reduction by a further factor of approximately 100. Having reduced the configuration space to around 2 × 10 6 structures, the authors can energetically order their structures. The authors perform DFT calculations on small subsets of the total number of structures to achieve results in a reasonable time frame. The first subset was the 200 energetically lowest structures according to the COMPASSIII forcefield. The second subset was a random selection of approximately 1000 structures across the entire configuration space to ensure good coverage. In total 1235 single point DFT calculations were performed. All DFT calculations were performed with the ONETEP code, where the computational cost scales linearly with the number of atoms as opposed to cubic scaling in conventional DFT. The authors use the PBE GGA exchange correlation functional and a kinetic energy cutoff of 830 eV.

Key Results
The authors found a correlation of 0.9996 when applying the MLR model to their test set. All structures are found to occur within a range of 5.8 eV of the lowest energy structure. Nineteen of the 20 lowest energy structures have a ratio of 8:48, with the 19th lowest being 9:47. The average energy for all structures occurs at 1.47 eV higher than the ground state structures. The average energy for each ratio increases with increasing 24d occupancy, indicating an energetic preference to avoid 24d occupation. There are four structures, all 8:48, within 0.026 eV (1 kT at 298 K) of the lowest energy structure. The four lowest energy structures have very similar atomic coordinates, all with the same 24d configuration with only slight variations in the 96h configuration. Geometry optimisation calculations on the final four structures find the energy gap between them narrows further. The 96h to 24d transition yielded the lowest overall energy structure (structure label 1095859), 0.58 eV lower in energy than the geometry optimised lowest energy single point structure. There is a negative correlation between the mean distance moved of all Li atoms and increasing energy of the final optimised c-LLZO structure. The most symmetric ratio appears to be 8:48 followed by 12:44 and finally 10:46. There does appear to be a slight correlation between lower energy and higher symmetry.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The energetic preference to avoid 24d occupation suggests that structures with 24d occupation are less stable, supporting the idea that the ground state avoids 24d occupation. The slight correlation between lower energy and higher symmetry suggests that symmetry may be a weak descriptor of energy, though including symmetry in the MLR model made a negligible difference. The negative correlation between the mean distance moved of all Li atoms and increasing energy suggests that movement from original sites is preferable to attain lower energies. The authors note that their energetic ordering procedure does not include entropic contributions and assumes a reasonable retention of ordering upon geometry relaxation, which are both approximations. The authors conclude that a large proportion of experimental and theoretical literature may be predicting or working with structures that are not reflective of a real system. The method could be extended to other ion conductors and partially occupied crystals, potentially improving accuracy and reproducibility in future research.

Contradictions And Limitations
The authors note that the majority of theoretical studies' 24d :96h ratio is likely not maintained after allowing their structure to relax or move, but the final ratio is rarely reported. The authors note that the choice of initial structure was mostly for convenience of a smaller phase space, and a low energy structure is not necessarily guaranteed even with AIMD. The authors note that coulombic forces alone are not sufficient to energetically order c-LLZO structures. The authors note that COMPASSIII predicts a more pronounced separation of energies depending on the 24d :96h ratio than is predicted by ONETEP, while good intra-ratio ordering is retained. The authors note that the trade-off for increased speed and lower memory costs is the high specificity of the method, which is limited to comparison of monoatomic sub-lattices with predefined positions. The authors note that a large-scale energy prediction of the geometry optimised structures falls outside the scope of this communication. The authors neglect to include the 48g site because it is not reported in most refinements, which may limit the completeness of the generated structures. The authors note that the method is limited to comparison of monoatomic sub-lattices with predefined positions, which may limit its applicability to other systems.

Claims
A workflow can identify energetically favourable configurations of c-LLZO, enabling the isolation of low-energy structures for a crystallographically predicted structure. The authors present a methodology to identify energetically favourable configurations of c-LLZO. The authors reduce the configuration space by eliminating symmetry images from all remaining structures. The authors perform 1235 single point DFT calculations to fit a multiple linear regression model. The MLR model achieves a correlation of 0.9996 on the test set. The authors provide all structures generated in a freely accessible database. The method could be extended to other ion conductors and partially occupied crystals. The authors note that the energetic ordering procedure does not include entropic contributions and assumes a reasonable retention of ordering upon geometry relaxation. The authors note that the majority of theoretical studies' 24d :96h ratio is likely not maintained after allowing their structure to relax or move. The authors note that a low energy structure is not necessarily guaranteed even with AIMD. The method could be extended to other ion conductors and partially occupied crystals. The authors provide all structures generated in a freely accessible database with the aim to improve accuracy and reproducibility in future c-LLZO research. The authors hope that in providing all possible structures they can bring further accuracy and reproducibility to future computational LLZO research.

Data And Code Availability
The authors provide all structures generated in a freely accessible database with the aim to improve accuracy and reproducibility in future c-LLZO research. The structures produced in this work are to be published alongside the results in the Supporting Information (SI) section. Both scripts for symmetry checking are provided with the database in the SI section. The DOI for the preprint is https://doi.org/10.26434/chemrxiv-2023-gz4d0. The license is CC BY-NC-ND 4.0.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The authors validated the symmetry checking methodology by comparing results against more rigorous methods using the ASE python package. The authors validated the method for both 13:43 and 12:44 ratios, with further discussion in the supporting information. The authors tested the effect of geometry relaxation on a small dataset of 20 structures. The authors tested including the symmetry of the structure in the MLR model and found it made a negligible difference to overall results. The authors performed 20 geometry optimisation calculations to assess the effect of geometry relaxed structures on the overall ordering. The authors found that none of the site changes (96h to 96h, 96h to 48g, and 96h to 24d) correlated significantly with the geometry optimised energy. The authors found that the 96h to 24d transition was only recorded once and yielded the lowest overall energy structure. The authors found that the 96h to 24d transition meant that the ratio of the structure changed from 9:47 to 10:46, the only time they observed such a feature. The authors found that the 96h to 48g and 96h to 24d transitions listed in order of frequency occurred. The authors found that the 96h to 24d transition yielded the lowest overall energy structure (structure label 1095859), 0.58 eV lower in energy than the geometry optimised lowest energy single point structure.

Ethical Considerations
The content is not peer-reviewed by ChemRxiv, as indicated by the license CC BY-NC-ND 4.0.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1b shows the c-LLZO structure with Li atoms partially occupying the 24d and 96h sites. Figure 1c shows the range of predicted structures in the literature, indicating disagreement about the ground state. Table 1 gives the number of structures for each 24d :96h ratio, for one unit cell. Figure 2b shows that 19 out of the 20 lowest energy structures have a ratio of 8:48. Figure 3 shows the workflow employed to find the 4 final structures from given occupancies. Figure S3 shows that COMPASSIII predicts a more pronounced separation of energies depending on the 24d :96h ratio than is predicted by ONETEP. Figure S4 shows the energy of a Li Dimer with changing inter-atomic distance, with the fit being a 3rd order polynomial. Figure S5 shows MLR energies compared to the order of the individual structure space group, for each 24d :96h ratio. Figure S7a shows a negative correlation between the mean distance moved of all Li atoms and increasing energy of the final optimised c-LLZO structure. Table S1 reports all experimental papers that explicitly report the site occupancies of the 24d and 96h sites. Table S2 reports all theoretical studies that explicitly report their 24d :96h ratio and a brief summary of how their structures were generated.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a workflow to identify energetically favourable configurations of c-LLZO, enabling the isolation of low-energy structures for a crystallographically predicted structure. 2. The strongest evidence is the correlation of 0.9996 achieved by the MLR model on the test set. 3. The future path is to extend the method to other ion conductors and partially occupied crystals, potentially improving accuracy and reproducibility in future research.
